title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Sustainably reducing aviation’s climate impact points toward alternative energy systems, with liquid hydrogen (H\(_2\)) and methane (CH\(_4\)) emerging as prime candidates for long-haul flight. However, these fuels differ substantially from Jet A in their leak and ignition behavior, requiring systemic safety considerations from the earliest design phases.
This research bridges three previously independent domains: certification frameworks, hazard physics, and aircraft performance. By coupling jet/flame consequence solvers (like HyRAM+) with multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO), we evaluate how passive leak-mitigation requirements impact transport efficiency across different fuel types and tank architectures.

title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Sustainably reducing aviation’s climate impact points toward alternative energy systems, with liquid hydrogen (H\(_2\)) and methane (CH\(_4\)) emerging as prime candidates for long-haul flight. However, these fuels differ substantially from Jet A in their leak and ignition behavior, requiring systemic safety considerations from the earliest design phases.
This research bridges three previously independent domains: certification frameworks, hazard physics, and aircraft performance. By coupling jet/flame consequence solvers (like HyRAM+) with multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO), we evaluate how passive leak-mitigation requirements impact transport efficiency across different fuel types and tank architectures.

title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Key Contributions & Technical Highlights

Designated Leak Zone (DLZ) Framework: Proposed formal classification of Designated Leak Zones (DLZs) for H\(_2\)- and CH\(_4\)-fueled aircraft—mirroring 14 CFR § 25.1181 for Jet A fire zones—to systematically handle unique alternative-fuel vapor and ignition risks.
Physics-Based Consequence Modeling: Utilized leak-consequence physics models to map out required ventilation mass flow rates and spatial separations needed to passively mitigate potential jet fires, explosions, and cryogenic-related damage.
Multidisciplinary Design Optimization (MDO) Integration: Developed an aircraft design procedure that optimizes vehicle configurations subject to leak safety constraints, allowing evaluation of transport energy as a function of fuel, tank layout, and mitigated leak rate (dubbed passive-threshold leak rate–PTLR).
Performance Impact Quantification: Demonstrated that flame-driven spatial separation requirements (especially for wing geometries) dominate system-level penalties over ventilation requirements, with CH\(_4\) producing higher penalties due to larger spatial offsets.

title: PhD Research: Hydrogen and Methane Aircraft Safety
text:
Results & Findings

Leak Behavior & Hazard Zones
Unlike Jet A—which forms slowly evaporating fuel pools with small ignitable regions—leaked H\(_2\) and CH\(_4\) vaporize quickly, mix readily with ambient air, generate larger ignitable regions, and feature lower ignition energies. Consequently, fuel tank spaces must maintain positive-pressure designs to prevent ignitable boil-off/air mixtures.

title: Dawn: High-Alitude Long Endurance Solar Aircraft for Ozone Monitoring
text: Completed as part of the MIT aerospace capstone (courses 16.82/821), the Dawn project focused on the design and prototyping of a solar-powered, high-altitude long-endurance (HALE) aircraft designed for ozone monitoring. This multi-semester effort included system-level propulsion modeling and hands-on composite manufacturing and structural testing to develop lightweight, high-performance components.

title: Dawn: High-Alitude Long Endurance Solar Aircraft for Ozone Monitoring

Propeller Manufacturing Prototyping: Fabricated custom composite propeller section layups to evaluate torsional stiffness performance, mass, and overall manufacturability.

Based in the Greater Boston area (Medford, MA), I am seeking full-time roles focused on aerospace R&D, systems engineering, and design/test engineering, especially those with a strong hands-on or physical hardware component.

title: Firefly: Deployable-Tail Micro-UAV
text:
As part of my S.M. research at the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, I led the design and development of the stability and control system for Firefly—a deployable micro-UAV powered by a slow-burning solid rocket motor.
The challenge involved engineering a reliable tail deployment mechanism that could transition seamlessly from a compact stowed configuration to a stable flying wing/tail architecture under changing vehicle static margin as the solid-rocket motor burned.






Figure 1: Firefly Concept of Operations.

title: Firefly: Deployable-Tail Micro-UAV
text:
As part of my S.M. research at the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, I led the design and development of the stability and control system for Firefly—a deployable micro-UAV powered by a slow-burning solid rocket motor.
The challenge involved engineering a reliable tail deployment mechanism that could transition seamlessly from a compact stowed configuration to a stable flying wing/tail architecture under changing vehicle static margin as the solid-rocket motor burned.






Figure 1: Firefly Concept of Operations.

title: Firefly: Deployable-Tail Micro-UAV
text:
Key Contributions & Technical Highlights

Folding-Tail Mechanism: Designed a pull-spring-actuated folding tail utilizing an oblique hinge that serves as both the physical deployment axis and the aerodynamic actuation axis.
Rapid Prototyping: Iterated rapidly through multiple 3D-printable vehicle iterations to test hinge mechanics, deployment reliability, and structural integrity.
Wind-Tunnel Testing: Built a custom pitch-balance test setup to experimentally evaluate longitudinal stability and controllability across various angles of attack.
Flight Testing: Conducted unpowered drop tests deployed from a quadcopter to collect stability and controllability data under glide conditions.
Validation: Correlated experimental wind-tunnel and drop-test data against analytical predictions generated via AVL (Athena Vortex Lattice).

title: Desktop Lathe: MIT Course 2.720 Team Project
text: This team hardware prototyping project, as part of MIT course 2.720, focused on the design, fabrication, and requirements verification of a custom desktop lathe. Precision mechanical design and rapid prototyping methods were employed to build a functional, benchtop-scale machining tool capable of turning stainless steel during the one semester long course.

title: Desktop Lathe: MIT Course 2.720 Team Project
text: This team hardware prototyping project, as part of MIT course 2.720, focused on the design, fabrication, and requirements verification of a custom desktop lathe. Precision mechanical design and rapid prototyping methods were employed to build a functional, benchtop-scale machining tool capable of turning stainless steel during the one semester long course.

title: Desktop Lathe: MIT Course 2.720 Team Project
text:
Key Contributions & Technical Highlights

Precision Manufacturing: Designed and machined aluminum and stainless steel spindle components and integrated the motor-to-spindle power transmission system.
Part & System Functional Requirements Verification: Post-manufacturing verification, using tools including a Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM), was conducted to verify parts met specified tolerances and stiffness requirements.

Iterative Pulley Geometry Prototyping: Designed and tested multiple crowned pulley geometries using 3D-printing to rapidly evaluate belt tracking and stability before committing to final fabrication geometry.
Functional Validation: Performed cut testing, successfully demonstrating the lathe’s capability to cleanly turn stainless steel stock.

title: Rocketry: MIT Rocket Team and Tripoli Certification Flights
text: Active involvement with the MIT Rocket Team included leadership roles as President and Propulsion Lead. The team focused on high-altitude solid-motor rocket flights utilizing in-house formulated and mixed solid rocket propellant alongside fully custom motors. In addition to team projects, personal rockets were designed and flown for Tripoli Rocketry Association certification, culminating in an L3 certification (the highest level) achieved with a scratch-built rocket.

title: Rocketry: MIT Rocket Team and Tripoli Certification Flights
text:
Key Contributions & Technical Highlights

President & Propulsion Lead, MIT Rocket Team: Served as President, leading approximately 80 students in the development of a P-class-motor rocket. Coordinated design reviews, acted as a liaison to MIT administration and industry partners, and secured FAA waivers for flights up to 80,000 ft. Also directed propulsion development as Propulsion Lead from January to July 2020.
Hobby Rocketry L3 Certification: Designed, scratch-built, launched, and successfully recovered an M-class solid-motor rocket to earn Tripoli Level 3 certification, achieving an altitude over 14,000 ft and a maximum speed of 950 mph.
